items.title: Young women widely believe that each person has a single ideal romantic partner destined for them, Turkish study finds
items.summary:
A small qualitative study of young heterosexual women in Turkey found that most endorsed the “one and only” romantic belief, the idea that each person has a single ideal partner or soulmate destined for them. The women generally viewed romantic relationships portrayed on social media as artificial and unrealistic, but the findings suggest that repeated exposure to such portrayals may still shape their romantic expectations in dysfunctional ways. The paper was published in BMC Psychology .

Romantic relationships are an important part of human life, but people’s expectations about love are shaped by cultural norms, gender roles, and media portrayals. Some people develop unrealistic romantic beliefs, such as the idea that true love lasts forever, that everyone has one perfect soulmate, or that love can overcome any obstacle. Such beliefs have been linked to lower relationship satisfaction, difficulties resolving conflicts, and a greater risk of experiencing psychological dating violence.

Movies, television series, and social media frequently portray romantic relationships in idealized ways, potentially reinforcing these unrealistic expectations. According to cultivation theory, repeated exposure to media messages can shape how people perceive reality, including what they expect from romantic relationships. Social media may be particularly influential because users frequently share carefully selected, idealized representations of their relationships.

Study author Gökçe Sancak Aydın of Yozgat Bozok University argues that culture plays a central role in romantic…

items.title: Flashy courtship traits tend to evolve faster than combat weapons, study finds
items.summary:
Decorative traits used to attract mates tend to evolve more rapidly than physical weapons used to fight rivals, according to new research published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B . Combining a mathematical model with data from 531 species in 10 animal groups, the researchers found that ornaments evolved faster overall, and their model suggests this is largely because mating preferences in the opposite sex drift unpredictably across generations. In the researchers’ framework, those shifting tastes create a moving evolutionary target for ornaments, whereas the physical demands of male-male competition keep weapons anchored to a steadier evolutionary pace.

Many of nature’s most elaborate features, from giant antlers to intricate courtship calls, persist not because they help an animal survive longer, but because they improve its odds of reproducing. Biologists call this evolutionary process sexual selection, and it operates through two primary channels.

Direct competition within the same sex, most often males fighting or intimidating rivals for access to mates, favors the evolution of weapons: physical structures capable of overpowering opponents or inflicting bodily harm, such as tusks, spurs, leg spines, and enlarged canine teeth. Mate choice, most often females choosing among prospective partners, favors the evolution of ornaments: visual, acoustic, or anatomical traits that appeal to a chooser’s senses, such as vibrant feathers, specialized vocal pitches, expandable throat fans, and elongated eye stalks.

Traits shaped by sexual selection often change faster over…
items.t: Flashy courtship traits tend to evolve faster than combat weapons, study finds

items.title: Scientists built an AI called “Concept2Brain” that simulates human brain waves from pictures and text
items.summary:
Scientists have developed an artificial intelligence tool called Concept2Brain that predicts how human brain waves respond to photographs or written text. In a study published in Nature Communications , the researchers report that the open-access platform generates synthetic electroencephalography (EEG) recordings that resemble real human brain activity during visual and emotional perception. The system could allow researchers to simulate brain-wave experiments on a computer before recruiting human volunteers.

Electroencephalography, or EEG, uses sensors placed on the head to measure tiny electrical voltage changes at the scalp produced by brain activity. Because this technique tracks neural activity millisecond by millisecond, scientists often repeat an image or event many times and average the time-locked EEG traces to isolate event-related potentials, which are characteristic wave patterns tied to seeing, thinking, or feeling.

In recent years, artificial intelligence has increasingly been paired with brain imaging to interpret what a person is experiencing. Much of that effort has focused on decoding, such as an fMRI study in which volunteers listened to stories, watched silent movies, or imagined narratives while a computer model reconstructed the general meaning of those stories from their brain scans.

Far less attention has gone to the reverse problem, known as encoding, in which a computer starts with an image or phrase and predicts the fast-moving scalp electrical waves an observer would produce. To make such predictions possible, neuroscientists first built…

items.title: Screens, inherited childhood scripts, and therapy skepticism lead this week’s psychology podcasts
items.summary:
Can you reset your brain’s reward system by unplugging for a day? One clinical psychologist argued in a rebroadcast this week that you can’t, while an addiction psychiatrist made the case for a month-long abstinence “experiment.” The two positions are not identical, but they pull in different directions on a question many listeners are asking about their phones and habits. Across 19 episodes from 13 shows, that conversation about dopamine sat alongside two other recurring threads: whether consciousness can be explained by the brain at all, and how childhood “scripts” carry into adult life.

The week’s other notable discussions include Scott Galloway putting his claim that therapy has been oversold to a psychologist, a neuroscientist explaining a theory that treats experience itself as the starting point, and a live panel making the case that fun deserves to be taken seriously.

Desire, Dopamine and Addiction 
 All In The Mind rebroadcast “Dopamine, detoxes and donuts” , in which clinical psychologist Dr Anastasia Hronis, author of The Dopamine Brain , explains what dopamine does for motivation, movement and behaviour. She discusses how technology platforms keep users engaged. She also argues that trendy 24-hour detoxes and “raw dogging” flights cannot reset a chemical the brain depends on.

On Huberman Lab , Stanford addiction psychiatrist Dr. Anna Lembke appears in “Overcome Addictions & Obsessions of All Kinds” . The long conversation covers her pleasure-pain balance model, digital media addiction among adolescents, and her argument for a 30-day abstinence period. A…

items.title: Coercion isn’t the only route to power among teens, study suggests
items.summary:
A study of Ontario high school students found that adolescents can gain social power through coercion, but also through cooperation, admired traits, friendships, and alliances, according to research published in Evolutionary Psychological Science .

Social power becomes especially important during adolescence, when peer status, dating opportunities, access to resources, protection from victimization, and influence within the group can all carry real social value. But power is not one dimensional. Some adolescents might gain it through dominance, intimidation, or coercion, while others may gain it through prestige, cooperation, admired qualities, or supportive relationships.

Tristan Chaderton Bowman and colleagues examined how different routes to power are connected to different forms of power-holding among adolescents. Prior research has often focused on coercive or competitive routes to adolescent power, including bullying and dominance, but whether cooperative strategies can also help adolescents gain influence in ways that benefit both the individual and the peer group is less understood.

The researchers recruited 458 adolescents between the ages of 14 and 18 from one high school in southern Ontario. The students were in grades 9 to 12, with an average age of 15.9 years, and 48% were girls. The study was part of the sixth wave of a larger project on peer relationships. Research assistants visited classrooms, and students completed the study on electronic tablets.

The study used peer-nomination measures, meaning students identified classmates in their grade who fit…
items.t: Coercion isn’t the only route to power among teens, study suggests

items.title: People with eco-friendly habits are rated as more appealing partners
items.summary:
People who practice environmentally friendly habits tend to be viewed as more desirable romantic partners than those who disregard the environment, according to new research published in Environmental Psychology Research . In the second of two online experiments, this appeal depended in part on the observer’s own outlook: individuals with stronger positive attitudes toward nature were especially drawn to eco-friendly partners for committed relationships and viewed environmentally wasteful people less favorably. The findings suggest that everyday green habits may act as social signals in dating, particularly among people who care about protecting the planet.

Pro-environmental behavior refers to everyday actions that reduce harm to the natural world or benefit it, such as sorting household recycling, driving an electric car, or avoiding disposable plastics. Beyond their ecological impact, visible green habits communicate information about a person’s character. Because sustainable routines often take extra time, effort, or money without an immediate personal payoff, observers tend to interpret them as signs of prosociality, meaning a willingness to cooperate and help others.

From an evolutionary perspective on human mating, cooperative and generous traits matter in partner selection because they suggest someone will be a supportive companion and dependable parent. Consistent with that idea, a 2021 two-part study found that shoppers described as buying sustainable products were seen as more generous and rated as more attractive for both casual and committed relationships.…
items.t: People with eco-friendly habits are rated as more appealing partners

items.title: Regret is rare among transgender youth who began hormone therapy, according to largest study of its kind
items.summary:
Most people who began hormone therapy as teenagers at a U.S. gender clinic and answered a follow-up survey said starting treatment had been the right decision, according to a cohort study published in JAMA Pediatrics . Even among former patients who eventually stopped taking hormones, more than four out of five still reported that starting treatment had been the right choice for them. Very few respondents reported regretting the decision or feeling harmed by it, providing longer-term clinical data amid ongoing policy debates over adolescent medical care.

Gender-affirming hormone therapy involves taking prescribed estrogen or testosterone to develop physical traits that align with a person’s gender identity rather than the sex they were assigned at birth. Estrogen promotes changes such as breast growth and softer skin, whereas testosterone deepens the voice and stimulates facial and body hair growth, with some of these effects becoming permanent over time. Transgender and gender-diverse youth, whose gender identities differ from their birth-assigned sex and may be binary (male or female) or nonbinary, make up an estimated 3.3% of teenagers in the United States, though fewer than 0.1% of U.S. adolescents receive hormone therapy.

Short-term studies have consistently reported mental health improvements among teenagers receiving these medications, the new study’s authors note. For instance, a 2020 study by two of those authors followed youth at the same clinic for one year after they started hormone therapy or puberty blockers and found reductions in depression, anxiety, and…
items.t: Regret is rare among transgender youth who began hormone therapy, according to largest study of its kind

items.title: Psychedelics show anti-inflammatory effects in sick animals but not healthy ones, meta-analysis finds
items.summary:
A systematic review and meta-analysis found that most laboratory and animal studies report anti-inflammatory effects of psychedelics, but mainly when inflammation is already present. In mice and rats, psychedelics reduced inflammatory markers in animals with induced inflammation but not in healthy animals, while the small number of human studies produced mixed results. The paper was published in Brain, Behavior, and Immunity .

Psychedelics are psychoactive substances that alter perception, mood, and thought processes. Some of the most widely used psychedelics include psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), and N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT). Although they are illicit in most jurisdictions, they are being studied for their potential to treat conditions that do not respond to existing treatments.

Using psychedelics in controlled therapeutic settings is called psychedelic therapy. Research suggests that it may provide lasting benefits for people with psychiatric and neurological conditions such as depression, anorexia, Parkinson’s disease, and migraine. Although most research has focused on how psychedelics affect the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in their effects on other bodily systems, particularly the immune system. This is important because inflammation can influence brain function and behavior, while prolonged inflammation is associated with an increased risk of psychiatric and neurological disorders.

Some researchers therefore suspect that the therapeutic benefits of psychedelics may partly result from their ability to regulate immune responses…
items.t: Psychedelics show anti-inflammatory effects in sick animals but not healthy ones, meta-analysis finds

items.title: Neuroscientists just found a hidden “fingerprint” in human memory
items.summary:
Electrical rhythms sweeping across the surface of the human brain do not just travel in straight lines when people form and recall memories, according to new research published in Nature Communications . Using direct brain recordings from neurosurgical patients, scientists found that these rhythms also organize into swirling spirals, expanding or contracting rings, and other intricate shapes that shift with both the stage of memory and the specific letter a person is viewing. Machine-learning models trained on these geometric patterns were able to tell apart different memory states and individual remembered items above chance levels.

The cerebral cortex, the folded outer layer of neural tissue covering the brain, plays a central role in memory, language, and perception. Within this tissue, groups of brain cells generate rhythmic electrical fluctuations called neural oscillations, which cycle several times per second. When the peak of one of these electrical cycles shifts progressively from one patch of cortex to neighboring patches over thousandths of a second, much like a ripple moving across water, neuroscientists call it a traveling wave.

Individual brain cells in the cortex are physically wired to many distant regions, and those connections cannot rewire themselves from second to second as a person’s task changes. The authors hypothesize that by sweeping across the brain’s surface in organized patterns, traveling waves may temporarily align the timing of specific neuron groups, allowing separated regions to communicate flexibly as mental demands shift.

items.t: Neuroscientists just found a hidden “fingerprint” in human memory

items.title: New study finds vulnerable narcissism is linked to harsher judgments of police stops, even polite ones
items.summary:
How people judge a traffic stop may reflect not only how the officer behaves, but also the personality traits they bring to the interaction. A new experiment published in the Journal of Experimental Criminology suggests that people higher in vulnerable narcissism tend to view police stops less favorably even when an officer is courteous and fair, whereas those higher in grandiose narcissism respond more positively when shown respect or spared a ticket. The findings indicate that everyday psychological differences are linked to how people evaluate police encounters, although overtly rude policing drew strongly negative reactions across the board.

Nearly 50 million people in the United States aged 16 or older had contact with the police in 2022. Traffic stops are the most common type of encounter that police initiate. Research in criminology consistently indicates that these encounters go more smoothly when officers practice procedural justice, an approach to policing centered on fair decision-making and respectful interpersonal treatment. In practice, procedural justice involves four behaviors: giving citizens a voice to tell their side of the story, explaining decisions neutrally and transparently, treating people politely and with dignity, and showing genuine concern for the public.

Fair policing tends to encourage cooperation, satisfaction, and views of officers as legitimate authorities, and one proposed reason is that respectful treatment signals that a person is a valued member of society. Even so, an officer’s objective conduct does not always match how a citizen…
items.t: New study finds vulnerable narcissism is linked to harsher judgments of police stops, even polite ones

items.title: Tracking the connection between bipolar disorder and sexual distress
items.summary:
People with bipolar disorder often experience changes in their sex lives alongside their mood shifts, but exactly how these symptoms connect over time has rarely been measured. A recent six-month study of newly diagnosed patients found that depressive symptoms correspond with lower sexual desire and increased distress about sex, while daily mood swings are linked specifically to higher sexual distress. The research was published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research .

Bipolar disorder is a mental health condition characterized by extreme shifts in a person’s mood and energy levels. These shifts manifest as distinct clinical episodes. During depressive episodes, individuals may feel intense sadness, lethargy, and a loss of interest in daily activities. During manic or hypomanic episodes, individuals experience elevated energy, impulsivity, and sometimes a decreased need for sleep.

Clinical observations frequently note that energy fluctuations influence a patient’s sexual life. The risk of sexual dysfunction is often elevated in psychiatric populations. Sexual function generally involves multiple phases, including an initial desire phase followed by arousal and physical climax. In clinical settings, the desire phase is particularly relevant for people with bipolar disorder because a sudden increase or decrease in sexual interest is a known symptom of the condition.

Another component of sexual health is sexual distress. This concept is distinct from physical sexual dysfunction. Sexual distress encompasses feelings of inadequacy, grief, frustration, and worry that arise…
items.t: Tracking the connection between bipolar disorder and sexual distress

items.title: A $1 LSD booklet from 1967 anticipated much of today’s psychedelic safety advice, study suggests
items.summary:
Nearly sixty years after an underground educator published a $1 mail-order booklet on how to avoid bad LSD trips, contemporary psychedelic users and facilitators still endorse almost all of her practical advice. A new survey study published in Psychedelics indicates that experienced users agreed on average with 18 out of 19 safety recommendations from Lisa Bieberman’s 1967 manual, suggesting that much of today’s harm reduction advice was already circulating in grassroots literature decades before modern clinical guidelines.

Psychedelics are mind-altering substances, such as psilocybin (the active compound in “magic mushrooms”) and lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), that temporarily produce profound shifts in perception, emotion, and thought. Psychedelic harm reduction refers to practical strategies aimed at lowering the psychological and physical risks of taking these drugs, rather than relying solely on abstinence. In practice, harm reduction focuses on preparing one’s mindset beforehand, arranging a calm and secure physical environment, and ensuring reliable emotional support during a session.

Growing public interest in clinical trials of psychedelic-assisted therapy has coincided with rising psychedelic use in the general population, most of which still occurs outside supervised medical settings. Although classic psychedelics carry relatively low risks of organ toxicity or addiction compared to many legal and pharmaceutical drugs, unsupervised trips can provoke acute panic, paranoia, confusion, and, in rarer instances, cardiovascular strain or severe psychiatric…
items.t: A $1 LSD booklet from 1967 anticipated much of today’s psychedelic safety advice, study suggests

items.title: Paid sexual exchanges are far more common among young adults than once thought, new study suggests
items.summary:
Over one-third of young adults in the United States report having provided in-person sexual acts or virtual sexual materials for financial compensation, according to a nationally representative survey published in The Journal of Sex Research . That 36% lifetime rate is more than four times the 8.3% rate captured by a traditional single question asked in the same survey, encompassing digital and physical exchanges ranging from consensual work to coerced exploitation. Young people reporting these exchanges also faced elevated rates of trauma, mental health struggles, and substance misuse.

Providing sexual acts or materials for financial compensation covers both physical encounters and digital exchanges provided for money or other payment. Physical forms include vaginal, oral, or anal sex, sexual touching, exotic dancing, and paid companionship, while virtual forms include sexting, phone sex, explicit photos or videos, and online companionship.

Measuring how often young people participate in these exchanges has been difficult because social stigma discourages disclosure and most large surveys rely on a single blunt question. For example, a 2016 national survey of U.S. adolescents and young adults asked a single question about trading sex for money, drugs, food, or shelter and estimated that roughly 5% had done so.

Single-question surveys overlook online platforms where young people sell explicit photos, videos, or messages without physical contact. Although virtual exchanges may avoid some physical risks like sexually transmitted infections, the authors note they are still…
items.t: Paid sexual exchanges are far more common among young adults than once thought, new study suggests

items.title: Tau builds up faster in people who develop Alzheimer’s before 65, large PET study finds
items.summary:
People who develop Alzheimer’s disease before age 65 tend to have more widespread buildup and faster spread of toxic tau protein in the brain than those who develop the condition later in life, according to a brain-imaging study published in Science Translational Medicine .

These differences persisted even after accounting for how cognitively impaired patients were at their initial scan, suggesting that early-onset Alzheimer’s involves a more aggressive form of tau accumulation. The researchers suggest the findings could have implications for how younger patients are treated, including the timing of amyloid-lowering drugs and the testing of therapies that target tau.

Symptom patterns and brain proteins in early- and late-onset Alzheimer’s 
 Alzheimer’s disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which brain cells gradually deteriorate and die, causing worsening problems with memory, thinking, and daily functioning. Clinicians classify the condition as early-onset Alzheimer’s when symptoms begin before age 65 and late-onset Alzheimer’s when symptoms appear after 65. Early-onset cases account for roughly 5 percent of all diagnoses, and only about 5 percent of those younger cases stem from known inherited genetic mutations, meaning most arise sporadically without a single known trigger.

Older patients typically experience trouble forming new memories as their main early symptom, whereas younger patients more often develop early difficulties with language, visual and spatial perception, or planning and decision-making, alongside faster cognitive decline. Inside…
items.t: Tau builds up faster in people who develop Alzheimer’s before 65, large PET study finds

items.title: Smartphone game shows promise as an add-on to antidepressants
items.summary:
A smartphone game designed to support people with depression, offered together with optional online therapy modules and on-demand therapist support, reduced depression and anxiety symptoms among adults who were already taking antidepressants, according to a randomized controlled trial in Sweden. Participants who received nine weeks of access to the program also reported better adherence to their medication than those on a waitlist, but their quality of life did not differ. The paper was published in the Journal of Affective Disorders .

Depression is a common mental disorder affecting approximately 300 million people worldwide. It reduces quality of life and creates substantial economic costs. Antidepressant medications are a common treatment for depression, but many patients continue to experience depressive symptoms despite taking them. Another major problem is that many patients do not take their prescribed medications regularly.

Internet-based cognitive behavioral therapy (ICBT) has emerged as an accessible treatment option. Research shows that it can be as effective as face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy in reducing depressive symptoms. Researchers are increasingly interested in combining antidepressant medications with digital psychological interventions delivered through smartphones.

One promising approach involves serious games. These games use elements of video games to encourage behaviors that support mental health. They may improve motivation and medication adherence by rewarding healthy behaviors and helping users establish daily routines. For example,…
items.t: Smartphone game shows promise as an add-on to antidepressants

items.title: AI-written peer reviews outscored top human experts in blind comparisons, Harvard working paper finds
items.summary:
A new study suggests that advanced artificial intelligence models can generate more thorough, accurate, and constructive peer reviews of unpublished academic papers than well-paid human experts operating under ideal conditions. In blind comparisons judged by an AI model and by former journal editors, the AI-written reviews won the large majority of matchups and contained about a third the rate of incorrect claims, according to a working paper posted online by Harvard University researchers.

The findings point to potential changes in how scientific journals evaluate research while raising questions about whether widespread reliance on AI could make scientific thinking more uniform.

The challenges of human and AI peer review 
 Peer review is the standard quality-control process in scholarly publishing, in which independent researchers in the same field read a draft of a scientific paper to help the authors improve their work and advise journal editors on whether the study merits publication. Despite its central role in science, the traditional review system struggles with frustrating delays, difficulties recruiting qualified volunteers, and low agreement between different experts evaluating the same manuscript. Human referees also frequently miss major errors, offer superficial feedback, or show bias toward familiar methods and prestigious institutions.

Recently, scholars have turned their attention to large language models, which are AI systems trained on vast collections of text to analyze and generate written language. However, applying these tools to scientific work…
items.t: AI-written peer reviews outscored top human experts in blind comparisons, Harvard working paper finds

items.title: Brain scans reveal structural differences in treatment-resistant schizophrenia
items.summary:
A recent study found that individuals with treatment-resistant schizophrenia exhibit specific structural differences in their brains, including a smaller hippocampus, compared to patients who respond to standard medications. These anatomical variations could eventually help doctors identify which patients are unlikely to benefit from typical antipsychotic drugs, allowing for earlier alternative interventions. The research was published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry .

Schizophrenia is a psychiatric condition characterized by hallucinations, delusions, and cognitive impairments. Standard antipsychotic medications primarily work by blocking dopamine receptors in the brain, which effectively reduces symptoms for many individuals. However, up to 60 percent of patients do not experience adequate symptom relief from these standard drug therapies. This condition, known as treatment-resistant schizophrenia, presents major challenges in psychiatric care.

The only medication currently approved for this specific population is clozapine. Its administration requires strict blood monitoring due to the risk of severe immune system complications, and a substantial portion of patients still fail to respond to it. Medical professionals currently diagnose treatment resistance only after a patient has failed to improve following multiple trials of different antipsychotic drugs. This trial-and-error process can take months or years, during which the patient’s mental health often deteriorates.

An objective biological marker could allow doctors to bypass this waiting period and initiate…
items.t: Brain scans reveal structural differences in treatment-resistant schizophrenia

items.title: Being near a romantic partner may help the body regulate blood sugar, temperature, and stress
items.summary:
Sharing a room with a romantic partner or caregiver may help the human body regulate basic internal functions, including blood sugar levels, skin temperature, and stress arousal, with less overall effort than when alone.

Across four experiments with adults and infants published in Science Advances , participants experienced smaller bodily disruptions and faster recovery during physical challenges when accompanied by a close companion. The findings suggest that social connection does not merely influence emotions and behavior, but also supports core biological maintenance from moment to moment.

Rethinking homeostasis as a social process 
 Every living organism must keep its internal environment within a narrow, healthy range despite changing conditions, a biological balancing act known as homeostasis. Managing body temperature, digesting food, and regulating nervous system arousal all consume energy, so meeting those demands with smaller spikes and quicker recovery, in the authors’ framework, leaves more resources for other vital bodily functions.

Evolutionary biologists and psychologists typically view group living through external benefits such as protection from threats, cooperation, reproduction, and emotional comfort under stress. Study lead author Monia Masalha and senior author Shir Atzil, an associate professor of psychology at The Hebrew University of Jerusalem who leads the Atzil Lab , worked with their colleagues to test a broader principle they call social physiology. Under this view, the physical presence of a close companion directly reduces the bodily…
items.t: Being near a romantic partner may help the body regulate blood sugar, temperature, and stress

items.title: Bedroom temperature may be a hidden drag on productivity, study suggests
items.summary:
Sleeping in a warmer bedroom during the summer is associated with poorer sleep quality and feeling less focused and productive the next day, according to new research published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology . By combining bedroom air sensors, wearable sleep rings, and smartwatch check-ins over several weeks, the researchers found that night-to-night increases in indoor heat corresponded with more restless sleep and small dips in self-reported daytime productivity. As nighttime temperatures climb globally, the findings point to bedroom temperature as an everyday factor tied to nightly rest and daytime focus.

Perceived productivity refers to how focused and capable of completing tasks a person feels during daily activities. The authors draw on models of work recovery, which propose that people need adequate rest to replenish the attention and self-control they use up during the day. They reasoned that if warm bedrooms degrade sleep quality, meaning how continuous, deep, and restorative a night’s sleep is, people may start the morning with fewer mental resources.

Warm weather can erode nightly rest and strain daytime work output, though those problems have mostly been studied apart. Globally, a 2022 study of more than seven million wearable sleep recordings estimated that rising temperatures cost people roughly 44 hours of sleep per year, while a 2018 meta-analysis of workers exposed to occupational heat linked thermal strain to worse health and lower job productivity. Direct tests of bedroom heat, sleep, and next-day thinking have largely used small climate…
items.t: Bedroom temperature may be a hidden drag on productivity, study suggests

items.title: Insecure attachment linked to reduced well-being in bisexual young adults
items.summary:
Young bisexual women face unique social pressures that can shape their mental health in both positive and negative ways. Research published in the International Journal of Sexual Health reveals that insecure relationship patterns predict increases in psychological distress and reductions in overall well-being over time for this demographic. The findings emphasize that evaluating mental health requires looking beyond the mere presence of distress to also consider what helps people thrive.

Traditional models of mental health have historically operated on a medical framework that defines wellness simply as the absence of mental illness. Psychologists have increasingly adopted an alternative approach known as a dual-perspective model. This framework treats psychological distress and positive well-being as distinct dimensions of human experience. A person might experience symptoms of depression while still maintaining a strong sense of life purpose, or they might lack psychological distress but still feel deeply unfulfilled.

Bisexual women often report elevated levels of psychological distress compared to heterosexual individuals and other sexual minority groups. Sociologists attribute this vulnerability to unique forms of stigma known as minority stress. Bisexual individuals frequently face discrimination from the heterosexual majority and simultaneously encounter invalidation from within the broader LGBTQ community. This dual marginalization can be especially intense during a person’s late teens and twenties, a developmental period when young adults are navigating major…
items.t: Insecure attachment linked to reduced well-being in bisexual young adults

items.title: How Couples Create Their Own Unique Microcultures
items.summary:
Do you have a pet name for your partner? I do, and many people I know do, too. Calling your loved one by a special nickname imbued with meaning—like “Bunny,” “Lumba,” or “Buncakes”—communicates in shorthand your unique connection and relational history.

Using pet names is just one example of what some researchers refer to as “ microculture ”—a combination of shared language, rituals, stories, histories, and more that evolve between small groups of people in close relationships and help sustain them. Maya Rossignac-Milon of Barcelona’s IESE Business School and her research collaborators are looking into how microculture could play a role in the very smallest of groups, romantic couples, and whether it holds clues to how these relationships thrive over time. 

“People experience this commonly, and our initial research suggests that it’s super pervasive,” says Rossignac-Milon. “We are basically proposing that attraction and, more importantly, relationship satisfaction is something that’s created together in the moment.”

What microculture means for relationships 

While much relationship research focuses on how individual traits (like extraversion, emotional expressiveness, or attachment style) affect relationship dynamics, Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues suggest that the development of microculture also plays an important part in couple formation, happiness, and relationship satisfaction.

“Two people can be quite different from each other, but, with microculture, they’re building something together that didn’t exist before their relationship, that’s totally unique to…
items.t: How Couples Create Their Own Unique Microcultures

items.title: The young women driving the US prenup boom: ‘I want to protect myself’
items.summary:
Zillennial couples say they want ‘radical transparency’ around their finances, bucking the idea that prenuptial agreements are rooted in division

Kai Amos does not know adult life without her fiance, Garret. They are high school sweethearts who met as teens in Idaho and moved across the country to New York together. They got engaged last year and will be married in September. Their days hum with the constant buzz of wedding planning: picking vendors, writing the guest list, dress shopping. And also meeting with lawyers; the happy couple are working on a prenuptial agreement, to protect their respective assets should they ever get divorced.

Amos, who is 30, understands the concept has baggage. Her more conservative friends and family back home in Idaho view prenups as something a rich man (and it is always a man) uses to rein in a woman he suspects of gold digging (and it is always a woman, usually younger). “It was always like the idea of a man trying to take advantage of a woman,” Amos said, “and therefore, it has this negative connection that the man is not going to be a trusted partner.”

items.title: The thermostat wars tearing couples apart: ‘It’s hard to feel sexy when you’re freezing cold’
items.summary:
Almost two-thirds of bedfellows disagree about the perfect room temperature – and the issue can affect office workers and housemates too. It oftens lead to subterfuge and skulduggery. So is there any way to reach a truce?

Recently I read an item on Threads that made me laugh out loud. “New dating app idea: post your thermostat settings to find your match.” The poster then revealed their own preferences: a balmy 24C by day and a chilly 19C at bedtime.

The suggestion elicited a rush of responses. “As someone who married outside their thermostat bracket, all I can say is that this is the most brilliant idea ever,” enthused one user. “Get outta here with that daytime terrarium,” responded another. “Are you storing pallets of produce in your house that you need to keep cold?” chimed in a third.

items.title: Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?
items.summary:
Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions. More recent studies of psychological well-being—also referred to as happiness, flourishing, thriving, or the good life (among other terms)—have been reporting positive links to health and longevity. 

For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”

That’s what Max Genecov and David S. Yeager explored in a recent meta-analysis , which combined findings from 99 different studies that measured mental health symptoms and conditions, well-being scores, and lifespan. Importantly, all the studies that they drew from used a longitudinal method, which means they took measurements repeatedly over time to explore whether momentary scores or score changes over time (e.g., well-being in early adulthood, or improvement in well-being) correspond with later scores or changes in another factor (such as the age or cause of death).

Well-being is generally understood as a combination of regularly feeling positive emotions, being satisfied with your life, and having a sense of meaning and purpose in life; ill-being reflects frequent and persistent negative emotions, chronic dissatisfaction, and purposelessness. 

To get at this question of whether mental ill-being and well-being over time had overlapping, combined, or independent effects on all-cause…
items.t: Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

items.title: Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?
items.summary:
In recent years, the language of therapy has moved beyond the clinic and into everyday conversation, giving us new ways to name our inner lives and, at times, new ways to misread them. Nowhere is this more evident than in how we respond to grief.

In grief, we learn quickly which words help and which ones wound. “At least they lived a long life.” “They wouldn’t want you to be sad.” Most of us recognize these as unhelpful sentiments.

Not all harmful responses to grief sound like clichés, though. Sometimes they arrive dressed in compassion, wrapped in the language of awareness. A friend might say, “This seems to be activating your abandonment wound,” “Maybe this pain is really about your father,” or “Maybe this is more about your unhappiness in your marriage.” The words may be well-intentioned, even psychologically accurate, yet the effect can be deeply unsettling. Instead of feeling seen, we feel studied; instead of comforted, diagnosed.

This dynamic can feel like a kind of gaslighting because the tools and language of healing are used to explain away your emotions instead of tending to them. Unlike gaslighting in the usual sense, it isn’t malicious. It’s the experience of being told what your pain really means instead of having that pain simply met. It is a byproduct of a therapy-literate culture that often privileges interpretation over presence. 

For the past several years, I’ve taught death and dying at the university level and led grief retreats. Again and again, I’ve watched grief ease, not when someone explained it, but when someone stayed with it. In what…
items.t: Are You Making This Common Mistake With Grief?
